bugs: If an abort listener on the timed-out attempt's signal calls cancel() while the task is 'retrying', failAttempt still emits the 'retry' event afterwards for a task that is already cancelled. The makeReady call is guarded; the emit is not.

onIdle() called from the last task's success/failure listener resolves before the 'idle' event is emitted, because it checks unfinished===0 rather than whether idle has been announced. Minor ordering inconsistency.
strengths: Clean module split: a generic Heap and an Emitter (snapshot iteration, per-registration unsubscribe, unknown-event check) are separate from the Scheduler.

Scales well. Ready heap with lazy deletion, an unmet-dependency counter instead of rescanning deps, and forwardRefs that let cycle detection skip the DFS unless a forward reference or self-dep exists, so a normal add costs O(deps).
All graph walks are iterative (cycle DFS, cascade, assignDependencyError), and a 20k-deep chain is tested.
Commit-then-emit discipline: state, cascade, slot release and abort all happen before any event, so listeners see final states.
Attempt object identity gives one stale-settlement check covering timeout, cancel and late settle.
Thorough input validation, including id, run and deps types.
weaknesses: The op/depth/idleEmitted interplay is subtle. Re-entrant cascade ordering with listeners (e.g. 'late' cancel before 'child' cancel) is documented but surprising.
NOTES references an external spec.md with a redacted path, so part of the rationale is not self-contained.
Cascade cause is the first dead dependency in deps order rather than the cascade path. This is defensible, but assignDependencyError adds a second walk.

bugs: findCycle is recursive and copies the path array at each level. Every add runs a full DFS: O(n^2) time and memory on long chains, and a stack overflow for very deep dependency chains (tens of thousands).
Registering the same listener function twice and calling the second unsubscribe removes the first registration, because it uses indexOf(listener).
Dispatch scans the whole queued Set for every slot fill, so it is O(queued) per start and O(n^2) overall with many ready tasks.
strengths: Compact and readable: a single dependents index handles forward refs, readiness and cascades.
The ready-transition sequence plus add-index tiebreak is a clear model of 'same moment'.
The 'busy' flag means onIdle() called mid-transition waits for the actual idle announcement.
attemptFailed guards against a re-entrant cancel from an abort listener before emitting 'retry'.
NOTES are thorough and explicit about every open-behaviour decision.
weaknesses: Algorithmic choices (linear scan, recursive cycle search on every add, depsSucceeded rescans) do not scale.
Test suite is thinner. No unhandled-rejection trap, a 20-microtask flush helper rather than a macrotask, and the cycle-content assertion is sorted.
No validation of id or deps types.
Timeout TaskError wraps a synthetic TimeoutError cause. This is allowed, but it is an extra type that consumers may not expect.

bugs: Cycle detection runs a full iterative DFS on every add, with no forward-reference shortcut, giving O(V+E) per add and O(n^2) to build a large graph.

With a zero-delay retry, the phase is never set to 'retrying'. A cancel issued from an abort listener or any reentrant path during the window sees the phase as 'running' with an already-ended attempt. Probably unreachable today, but the invariant is fragile.
A re-entrant cancel during a timed-out attempt's abort can still deliver the queued 'retry' event after the task is cancelled.
strengths: Discriminated-union Phase carries per-state data (attempt, timer handle, value/error). This makes illegal states hard to represent, and state() is just phase.kind.
Heap entries hold the phase object identity, so staleness detection is elegant and exact.
Fully iterative graph walks, and Object.fromEntries for ctx.deps (__proto__-safe, and tested).

An exceptional test suite: harness helpers (controlled/scripted/instant), exact event-sequence assertions, timer accounting, a global timer/Date.now spy, unhandled-rejection traps with real macrotasks, re-entrancy cases, and a mutation-testing script.
NOTES clearly separate PO-confirmed decisions from self-made ones and describe test provenance.
weaknesses: The deferred event queue (emit enqueues, flush delivers) adds a second layer of ordering semantics. A nested call returns before its own events are delivered, which is harder to reason about.
All logic, including the heap, lives in one file. This is less modular than X.
Validation does not cover id, run or deps types. The duplicate check precedes validation, which is unusual but documented.

result.rationale: X and Z are both high-quality, correct-looking implementations with iterative graph handling, heap-based ready queues and careful commit-then-emit semantics. X edges ahead on design: its module split and its O(deps) add path, thanks to the cycle-check shortcut and unmet counters, scale better. Z has the more expressive state model and by far the strongest test suite, including mutation testing and global-timer spies. Y is clean and well documented, but its linear dispatch scan, recursive per-add cycle search (stack overflow on deep chains) and comparatively thin tests make it clearly the weakest. The remaining bugs are minor re-entrancy edge cases common to X and Z, plus a listener-unsubscribe identity issue in Y.
